solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: In conflict we laid down guns, finally ousted by monarch, hurt?

indicators.note: things in conflict are in disarray, so the fodder letters are scrambled
the final letter of the fodder phrase is pushed out and something else takes its place

parts.note: K is the abbreviation for king, a monarch

explanation.surface: Soldiers in a war have put down their weapons and been removed by the king, and are they injured?
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally ousted by monarch' swaps the last letter of 'guns' for K, giving WELAIDDOWNGUNK, which 'In conflict' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Casualties able to walk despite injury are collectively called by this phrase, so it describes the hurt.

clue.text: Inform about nuclei undergoing fission

indicators.note: splitting apart breaks the word up, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A briefing about atomic nuclei splitting in a reactor.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone the key information about something is the phrasal verb meaning to inform them.

clue.text: Wrapping not quite 8, also so long?

indicators.note: the word for also is placed around the other piece, enclosing it

parts.note: too means also

indicators.note: not quite the whole word, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: the answer to 8 across, a word meaning a lot

explanation.surface: A puzzling question about something not quite wrapped up, also lengthy.
explanation.walkthrough: The 8 refers to the answer at 8 across; 'not quite' drops its last letter. The answer is an old-fashioned British way of saying goodbye.
explanation.definitionFit: A jaunty dated British farewell, equivalent to goodbye or cheerio, said when parting.

clue.text: Cooking ingredient came for errant sailors

indicators.note: errant means wandering astray, so these letters stray into a new order

parts.note: a tar is a sailor, so two of them give the plural

explanation.surface: Someone came to collect wayward seamen.
explanation.definitionFit: Potassium bitartrate, a white powder used in baking to stabilise egg whites, is a kitchen ingredient.

clue.text: I'll get caught by rabid pet on tiptoe

indicators.note: one piece is held inside the other, as if caught
rabid means wild or mad, so the letters go wild into a new order

parts.note: I'll gives the letter I, the 'will get' doing the linking

explanation.surface: A warning about being bitten by a mad pet while creeping on tiptoe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'll get caught' reads as a person being caught, but only the letter I is used; 'rabid' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: In ballet, dancing on the tips of the toes is called by this French term, a form of tiptoe.

clue.text: Relies on farcical setting for play

indicators.note: a farce is chaotic, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Someone depends on a ridiculous stage set for a production.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet takes place at the Danish castle of this name, so it is the setting for Shakespeare's play.

clue.text: Monopolised by FT compilers? O, no! We went down on them!

indicators.note: the exclamation 'O, no!' says the letter O is not wanted, so it is removed

parts.note: what the Financial Times setters keep entirely to themselves is, in their words, all of ours

explanation.surface: Setters for the Financial Times lament that they crawled about on something they had cornered.
explanation.walkthrough: The setters speak: something they monopolise is 'all of ours'; 'O, no!' drops the O of 'of'. Crawling on hands and knees is going down on all fours.
explanation.definitionFit: Crawling people get down on hands and knees, so the phrase names what they went down on.

clue.text: Simpletons executed a lot

indicators.note: executed means beheaded here, so the first letter is cut off

parts.note: noodles is slang for fools or simpletons

explanation.surface: A large number of fools were put to death.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial word for a great quantity or plenty of something.

clue.text: I mean to say Bless You x

definitions.text: I mean to say Bless You
definitions.meaning: a priest traces a cross in the air to convey a blessing
an x is the mark people who cannot write traditionally make as a signature

explanation.walkthrough: The 'x' looks like a kiss at the end of a message, but it is a mark made in place of a signature.
explanation.definitionFit: Tracing a cross bestows a blessing, and an x, the cross-shaped mark, was how the unlettered signed.

clue.text: Dug-out not required for this generator's activity

definitions.text: Dug-out not required for this generator's activity

parts.words: Dug-out not required for this generator's activity
parts.note: a dug is an udder or teat, so feeding a baby without one, from a flask with a teat, needs no dug out

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dug-out' suggests a trench or a baseball shelter; here it is a dug (teat) brought out, and the 'generator' is a parent.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeding an infant from a bottle of milk rather than at the breast, so no udder or teat is bared.

clue.text: Massage divers naked

indicators.note: divers is an old word meaning various or sundry, so the letters take varied positions

explanation.surface: A massage given to naked swimmers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'divers' is not people who dive but the archaic adjective meaning sundry.
explanation.definitionFit: Working and pressing muscles with the hands is to massage them, like working dough.

clue.text: Like poetical (spring?) hares in huge numbers?

definitions.meaning: poetry puts an a- before a verb, as in a-hunting, so leaping spring hares are a-leaping

explanation.walkthrough: Read as A-BOUNDING, the poetic prefix a- on bounding, the way hares leap in spring.
explanation.definitionFit: Being present in great quantity or plentiful is what teeming in huge numbers means.

clue.text: Real fddler fxing on the end

indicators.note: the pieces are fixed into the middle of the other word, set firmly inside it

parts.note: the emperor Nero is said to have fiddled while Rome burned
Z is the end of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A genuine violinist is mending the final part.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as held reads 'fddler' and 'fxing' for fiddler and fixing.
explanation.definitionFit: In mathematics a real quantity that is not nothing; here it means actual, having some value.

clue.text: I used to paint and draw explorer

parts.note: a tie is a drawn game
Marco Polo, the Venetian traveller to China

explanation.surface: A former painter speaks, then sketches a famous traveller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I used to paint' is the definition, spoken by the dead painter: Giambattista Tiepolo, the Venetian fresco artist.
explanation.definitionFit: The eighteenth-century Venetian painter Giambattista, speaking in the first person, painted in his lifetime.

clue.text: The latest information on future soap storylines?

definitions.meaning: a TV soap such as Coronation Street might reveal what is said on its street

explanation.walkthrough: Coronation Street is a long-running British TV soap opera, so script news about it could be the talk on the street.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for current rumour or news that is circulating.

clue.text: Runner restricts reformation of EEC fence

indicators.note: the river word hems in the other piece

parts.note: a river is a runner, as it runs

indicators.note: a reformation reshapes something, so these letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: An athlete curbs a reorganisation of the European Economic Community's barrier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' suggests an athlete, but a river runs; 'fence' is slang for a receiver of stolen goods.
explanation.definitionFit: A fence is slang for a dealer in stolen goods, someone who takes stolen property.

clue.text: General hitch overcome by woman of the night

indicators.note: in a down answer, one piece sits on top of the other

parts.note: tom is slang for a prostitute
to thumb a lift is to hitch

explanation.surface: Hitchhiking undone by a streetwalker.
explanation.walkthrough: General Tom Thumb was the stage name of Charles Stratton, the tiny star of P. T. Barnum's shows.
explanation.definitionFit: The diminutive performer Charles Stratton was billed by Barnum with the title of General.

clue.text: Not obvious an ulcer burst

indicators.note: something burst breaks apart, scattering the letters

explanation.surface: A ruptured ulcer may not be evident.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unclear is ambiguous or hard to make out, so it is not obvious.

clue.text: Finally, three year old breaks before donkey

indicators.note: the last letter of the following word is taken
the pieces break into the other word, sitting inside it

parts.note: ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: At last a three-year-old horse breaks clear before a donkey.
explanation.walkthrough: Eeyore is the gloomy donkey in A. A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh stories.
explanation.definitionFit: The melancholy grey donkey friend of Winnie-the-Pooh in Milne's books.

clue.text: Seems an alternative in a body

indicators.note: an alternative arrangement of the letters is required

explanation.surface: Apparently there is another option in an organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: A French-derived phrase meaning all together as a group, or collectively.

clue.text: Congress takes in space and time: material for terrorists

indicators.note: the outer word swallows the inner pieces

parts.note: congress can mean sexual intercourse
an em is a printer's unit of space

explanation.surface: A legislature is taking up space and time with talk of bombers' supplies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Congress' suggests the US legislature but means sexual intercourse.
explanation.definitionFit: A plastic explosive notoriously favoured by terrorist bombers.

clue.text: Churn-fller's passport, say, following a lot back

indicators.note: this piece comes after the other in the answer
the phrase is read from end to start

parts.note: a myriad is a great many, a lot
a passport is an example of ID, identification

explanation.surface: A butter-churn filler's travel document comes after a great many returns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the whole phrase 'a lot' around, giving the opening letters; 'following' places the passport piece after them.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who works in a dairy would fill churns with milk.

clue.text: Duff consumer? He'll be back!

definitions.meaning: ... Simpson in the TV cartoon drinks Duff beer
a homing pigeon always returns to its loft

explanation.walkthrough: 'Duff' looks like 'useless' but is the brand of beer in The Simpsons.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the cartoon father who drinks Duff and a homing pigeon, which flies back, share this name.

clue.text: Gloomy doctor takes year off

indicators.note: off means wrong or awry, so the letters go askew

explanation.surface: A depressed physician takes a twelvemonth's leave.
explanation.definitionFit: Dull, bleak and depressing, which is what gloomy means.

clue.text: Coding system for consumers — loads caught out

indicators.note: the abbreviation is taken out of the longer word

parts.note: to encumber is to load or burden
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A labelling scheme for shoppers with many items left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the code numbers for food additives printed on packaging.
explanation.definitionFit: The European numbering scheme for food additives is a code read on labels by consumers.
